title: My Mother-in-Law Downplayed My Baby's Hospital Stays So She Could Play House
excerpt: PART 1Today is my mother-in-law's birthday, and I'm not sending her a text. I'm not calling her, I'm not signing a card, and to be honest, I never want ...
author: admin

blocks.text: Today is my mother-in-law's birthday, and I'm not sending her a text. I'm not calling her, I'm not signing a card, and to be honest, I never want to see her again.

People act like you're supposed to forgive family no matter how many times they cross the line, especially when a new baby is involved. They tell you to be the bigger person. I tried that. I bit my tongue for months while she pushed and pushed, and two weeks ago I finally hit my limit.

My daughter, Lily, is thirteen weeks old today. Out of those thirteen weeks, she has spent about eight of them in the hospital. She was born with severe health issues, the kind that make you memorize the sound of every monitor beep and hold your breath every time a doctor walks into the room with a clipboard.

She spent her first three weeks in the NICU before we were even allowed to bring her home. Since then, we've been right back through those hospital doors over and over again. Watching a baby that small fight to get through the night changes how you see everything. You stop caring about who feels left out, and you only care about keeping your child alive.
My mother-in-law, Brenda, never seemed to get that. Looking back, the signs were there before Lily was even born.

When I was seven months pregnant, my husband, Mark, and I hadn't even cleared out our spare bedroom yet. We were still pricing cribs and waiting for the painter to call us back. Then Brenda invited us over for Sunday dinner and told us she had a surprise upstairs.
She led us down the hall and pushed open the door to her guest room.

The queen bed was gone. In its place was a brand-new white crib, a changing table, a rocking chair, and pale yellow curtains. There were folded receiving blankets stacked neatly on the dresser and a mobile hanging over the mattress.
I stood in the doorway looking at Mark, waiting for him to say something, because I thought maybe he'd talked to her about it. He looked just as confused as I was.

"I know you two are busy," Brenda said, smoothing down the crib sheet with both hands. "And I want to babysit three days a week once you go back to work. Tuesday, Wednesday, and Thursday. So I figured she'll need a proper room here."
She hadn't asked us. Not once. She hadn't asked if we even wanted help three days a week, or if I was going back to work right away, or what our plans were.
She just built a whole nursery in her house before we'd even built one in ours.

I should have spoken up right then. That's on me. I didn't want to ruin dinner, and I didn't want to look ungrateful when she'd clearly spent a lot of money. So I smiled, said the yellow paint was pretty, and changed the subject. Mark told me on the drive home that we'd sort it out later, once the baby arrived.
Then Lily arrived, and everything we thought our life would look like went out the window.

Those first three weeks in the NICU were a blur of hand sanitizer, plastic gowns, and sleeping in vinyl chairs. Brenda came to the hospital once during that stretch, stood outside the glass for twenty minutes, and complained on the phone to Mark afterward that the nurses wouldn't let her hold Lily.

Even after we got discharged, we weren't out of the woods. Lily's breathing would drop out of nowhere, or she'd stop taking her bottle, and we'd be packing an overnight bag at two in the morning to head back to the pediatric floor.
Every time we called Brenda to update her, she had the same reaction. She'd sigh, say babies are tougher than doctors give them credit for, and ask when she could come get her for the afternoon.
I kept telling myself she was just worried in her own way. I kept trying to be patient.

Then, two weeks ago, she came over to our house on a Tuesday afternoon. Lily had been home from her latest hospital stay for only four days. She was asleep in her bassinet in the living room, still tired, still fragile.
Mark was in the kitchen making coffee, and I was folding laundry on the couch, trying to stay quiet so the baby could rest.
Brenda walked into the living room, looked at Lily, and said, "Well, she looks fine to me. You two are keeping her locked up in here like she's made of glass."
I stopped folding and looked at her. "Brenda, she just got discharged on Friday. Her doctors said no unnecessary outings and no extra people around her right now."

"Doctors always say that to scare new mothers," Brenda said, waving a hand like I was being silly. "If you let her get some normal air and spend time at my house, she'd perk right up. That room I built is just sitting there collecting dust."
Mark walked out of the kitchen holding two mugs and heard the last part. "Mom, we've told you.
It's not about the room. She's been in the hospital more than she's been home."
Brenda's face tightened. She didn't look sorry. She looked annoyed, like Lily's medical records were an excuse we'd made up to spite her.
"You're keeping the baby from me," she snapped, pointing a finger toward the bassinet. "I've only seen her three or four..."

She didn't even get the last word out before Mark stepped between us and told her to lower her voice. I was shaking, partly from anger and partly from pure exhaustion. That was the moment I realized Brenda didn't want to hear the truth about her granddaughter. She just wanted to play house.
"Three or four times," I finished for her, keeping my voice low so I wouldn't wake Lily. "Yes, Brenda.
Because she has spent eight weeks of her life in a hospital bed. Where were you supposed to see her? At the pediatric ICU?"
Brenda crossed her arms. "I offered to sit with her at the hospital. You said only parents were allowed back there most days."

"Because that's the hospital rule," Mark said. His voice was tight, the way it gets right before he loses his patience. "We didn't make that up, Mom. You're talking to us like we're hiding her from you for fun."

"Well, it sure feels like it," Brenda said. She looked right at me, not at Mark. "Every time I call, it's another reason I can't take her. Another appointment. Another test. You two hover over that baby until she can't even breathe on her own."

All those weeks of sleeping in chairs next to oxygen tubes, watching nurses try to find a tiny vein in Lily's foot, eating cold crackers out of vending machines while praying her numbers would come back up, and Brenda was standing in my living room acting like I was making my own baby sick just to keep her away from a yellow guest room.
"I think you need to leave," I told her.

"I'm not leaving until we talk about next month," Brenda said. "When are you going back to work? Because I told my bridge group I'm watching her Tuesdays through Thursdays, and I already bought a spare car seat."
Mark set his coffee mug down on the table hard enough that it sloshed over the rim. "Mom. Stop. Nobody asked you to buy a car seat. Nobody asked you to build a nursery.
And nobody is driving Lily forty minutes to your house three days a week."

Brenda stood there for a few seconds, looking back and forth between the two of us like she couldn't believe Mark was actually siding with me. Usually, when she pushed hard enough, Mark would smooth things over and tell me to just let it go. This time, he didn't.

She grabbed her purse off the chair, walked out the front door, and let it click shut behind her. She didn't slam it, which somehow felt worse. It felt like she was just waiting for us to come to our senses and call her to apologize.
We didn't call. For the next ten days, the house was quiet. Lily had a good stretch, no fever, steady feeding, and a follow-up with her specialist that went better than the last one.
For the first time in months, I felt like I could take a full breath.

Then, four days ago, Mark's aunt Carol, Brenda's younger sister, called Mark while he was at the grocery store. When he came home, he put the bags on the counter and stood there with his keys still in his hand.
"Carol asked me why we won't let Mom help," he said.
I leaned against the doorway. "What did she mean by that?"

"She said Mom told everyone at her church lunch last Sunday that Lily is basically fine now," Mark said. He rubbed the back of his neck. "She told them the hospital stays were just routine newborn checks that got blown out of proportion, and that you're being overly controlling and won't let her use the nursery she spent two thousand dollars building."
Just tired, deep in my bones. Brenda wasn't just ignoring how sick Lily was when she talked to us. She was rewriting the whole thing to make herself look like the victim to the rest of the family.
"Did you tell Carol the truth?" I asked.
"Yeah," Mark said. "I sent her a picture of Lily's discharge summary with the dates highlighted and told her to ask Mom why she didn't mention the NICU."
Carol texted me an hour later to say she was sorry and that she hadn't known how serious it was. That helped a little, knowing at least one person in his family wasn't buying Brenda's version.

Still, it didn't fix the fact that Brenda had stood in front of her friends and called my daughter's hospital stays "routine checks" just so she wouldn't look foolish for building a nursery nobody asked for.
Three days later, Mark's phone started buzzing early in the morning. Today is Brenda's birthday, and Mark's cousin was planning a family lunch at a diner near Brenda's house.
I was sitting on the couch with Lily on my chest when Mark walked in from the kitchen holding his phone out so I could see the screen. It was a text from Brenda, sent directly to him.
"I hope you're bringing Lily to lunch today," the message read. "Everyone is asking to meet her, and I want to take a birthday picture with my granddaughter in her nursery afterward.
Tell your wife we can put the argument behind us today."
"Tell your wife," I said out loud. She couldn't even use my name.
"We're not going," Mark said right away. "I already told my cousin last night it was just going to be me dropping off a card."
"You don't even have to go for the card," I said.
